questions.q: The higher heating value (HHV) of a fuel assumes that:
c: Water formed is condensed to liquid
questions.e: HHV includes the latent heat of the water vapor, which is recovered when the water condenses to liquid.

x.A: Water staying as vapor is the lower heating value, since the latent heat is not counted.
x.B: HHV counts the latent heat released when the water formed in combustion condenses to liquid.
x.C: A fuel with no hydrogen would form no water, so the vapor-or-liquid question would not even arise; HHV does not assume this.
x.D: Excess air changes flue gas temperature and boiler efficiency, not how heating value is defined.

questions.q: What is the primary constituent of natural gas?
questions.e: Natural gas is mostly methane (CH4), typically 85–95%.

x.A: Ethane is only a minor component, usually a few percent.
x.B: Propane is a small component, normally separated out as LPG.
x.C: Methane is the main component, typically 85–95%.
x.D: Butane is a trace component, also separated as LPG.

questions.q: What is the reason producer gas requiring more air than natural gas?
questions.e: Producer gas has a much lower heating value, so a larger volume of gas (and its combustion air) is needed for the same heat output. Marked answer on the paper.

x.A: Producer gas has a much lower heating value, so a larger volume of gas is burned per unit of heat, which the marked answer ties to its air demand.
x.B: Density does not set the air a fuel needs; that comes from its combustible content.
x.C: Pressure does not change the chemical amount of air a fuel needs.
x.D: Temperature changes air density, not the oxygen needed for the fuel.

questions.q: The Orsat apparatus is used to measure:
questions.e: The Orsat apparatus analyzes flue gas by absorbing CO₂, O₂ and CO in turn.

x.A: Calorific value is measured with a bomb calorimeter, not an Orsat apparatus.
x.B: An Orsat apparatus absorbs CO₂, O₂ and CO from a flue-gas sample in turn to find its composition.
x.C: Flash point is found with a flash-point tester such as Pensky-Martens.
x.D: Moisture content is found by drying a sample and weighing it.

questions.q: The main cause of smoke in combustion is:
questions.e: Not enough air means incomplete combustion, so unburned carbon shows up as smoke.

x.A: Excess air gives more complete combustion and does not produce smoke.
x.B: Too little air leaves carbon unburned, and it leaves the stack as smoke.
x.C: Low sulfur reduces SO₂ and corrosion but has no effect on smoke.
x.D: Hydrogen burns readily to water vapor, so hydrogen-rich fuels tend to burn cleaner.

questions.q: In boiler combustion, a low CO₂ percentage with high O₂ indicates:
questions.e: Extra air dilutes the flue gas, which lowers the CO₂ percentage and raises the O₂.

x.A: Perfect combustion would show high CO₂ and very little leftover O₂.
x.B: Extra air dilutes the flue gas, lowering CO₂ and raising O₂.
x.C: Deficient air gives low O₂ and often CO, so O₂ would not be high.
x.D: High CO shows up when air is short, with little O₂, not a lot of it.

questions.q: ASTM D240 is the standard test for:
c: Heat of combustion of liquid hydrocarbons
questions.e: ASTM D240 measures the heat of combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuels with a bomb calorimeter.

x.A: Flash point is covered by ASTM D93 (Pensky-Martens), not D240.
x.B: D240 measures the heat of combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuels with a bomb calorimeter.
x.C: Sulfur in coal is covered by other coal tests (for example ASTM D3177).
x.D: Smoke point of kerosene is a different test (ASTM D1322).

questions.q: Which solid fuel generally has the highest volatile matter?
questions.e: Peat is the lowest-rank solid fuel, so it has the highest volatile matter (anthracite has the lowest).

x.A: Anthracite has the lowest volatile matter and the highest carbon.
x.B: Bituminous coal has moderate volatile matter.
x.C: Lignite is high in volatile matter but ranks above peat.
x.D: Peat is the lowest-rank solid fuel, so it has the highest volatile matter.

questions.q: For safe storage of liquid fuels, the container should be:
questions.e: The container must be sealed to limit vapor escape but vented so pressure from temperature changes can be released.

x.A: An unvented container can build pressure as temperatures change and rupture.
x.B: The container is sealed to limit vapor loss but vented to release pressure.
x.C: Heating continuously raises vapor pressure and fire risk.
x.D: A transparent container exposes the fuel to sunlight and heat and is not a safety requirement.

questions.q: The ASTM standard for coal proximate analysis is:
questions.e: ASTM D3172 covers proximate analysis of coal and coke (moisture, volatile matter, fixed carbon, ash).

x.A: ASTM D3172 covers proximate analysis of coal and coke: moisture, volatile matter, fixed carbon and ash.
x.B: D240 is the heat of combustion of liquid hydrocarbons, not coal proximate analysis.
x.C: D86 is distillation of petroleum products.
x.D: D93 is the flash point test.

questions.q: What is meant by “variable load” in a power plant?
c: Fluctuation in electrical demand over time
questions.e: Variable load is the change in electrical demand on the plant over time.

x.A: A sudden change in steam quality is an operating upset, not a definition of load.
x.B: Variable load means the electrical demand on the plant changes over time.
x.C: Drum-level variation is a boiler control matter, not a load definition.
x.D: A change in fuel composition is a fuel-quality issue, not load.

questions.q: Given two plants of similar capacity where one has lower load demand and the other has higher load demand. Which plant operates more efficiently?
questions.e: A higher load factor means the plant runs closer to its rated capacity, so it is used more fully and efficiently.

x.A: A higher load factor means the plant runs closer to its capacity, so it is used more fully and efficiently.
x.B: A lower load factor means the plant sits partly idle and is used less efficiently.
x.C: The two are not equal, because how fully each is used differs.
x.D: Fuel type affects cost, but load factor is what shows how fully a plant is used.

questions.q: Which control method is commonly used to match generation with variable electrical load?
questions.e: Automatic generation control (AGC) adjusts generator output to follow changing demand.

x.A: Boiler blowdown control removes dissolved solids from boiler water; it does not follow demand.
x.B: Automatic generation control adjusts generator output to follow changing demand.
x.C: Condenser vacuum adjustment tunes turbine back pressure, not generation to load.
x.D: An economizer bypass controls feedwater heating, not load matching.

questions.q: What is “spinning reserve” in variable load management?
c: Reserve of fuel oil in storage tanks
Backup capacity kept running and synchronized
questions.e: Spinning reserve is generating capacity that is already online and synchronized, ready to pick up load quickly.

x.A: Equipment kept offline is not spinning; it is non-spinning or cold reserve.
x.B: Spare condenser tubes are maintenance spares, not generating capacity.
x.C: Fuel oil in tanks is fuel inventory, not generating capacity.
x.D: Spinning reserve is generating capacity already online and synchronized, ready to pick up load quickly.

questions.q: What is “load factor” in power plant economics?
c: Ratio of maximum demand to average demand
Ratio of average load to maximum demand
Ratio of base load to peak load
Ratio of installed capacity to connected load
questions.e: Load factor = average load / maximum (peak) demand over a period.

x.A: That ratio is the inverse of load factor.
x.B: Load factor is average load divided by maximum demand over a period.
x.C: The base-to-peak ratio is not the definition of load factor.
x.D: Installed capacity against connected load is a different ratio.

questions.q: What is the relation between variable load operation and plant maintenance cost?
questions.e: Frequent load changes cause thermal and mechanical cycling, which increases wear and maintenance cost.

x.A: Cycling does not reduce wear, so maintenance cost does not fall.
x.B: Maintenance cost does not stay constant, because thermal cycling adds stress.
x.C: Frequent load changes cause thermal and mechanical cycling, which raises wear and maintenance cost.
x.D: Maintenance cost never becomes negligible under cycling.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of peak-load plants in a variable load system?
c: To provide base power at constant rate
To supply extra power during demand peaks
To dry the fuel before combustion
questions.e: Peak-load plants (such as gas turbines or diesel sets) run only when demand is high.

x.A: Providing base power at a constant rate is the job of base-load plants.
x.B: Peak-load plants, such as gas turbines or diesel sets, run only when demand is high.
x.C: Condenser vacuum is controlled by turbine auxiliaries, not peak-load plants.
x.D: Fuel drying is a fuel-handling function, not peak-load duty.

questions.q: Which type of control valve is preferred for fast response in variable load steam lines?
questions.e: Marked answer on the paper. Globe valves give good throttling and control of flow, which is why they are used in control service.

x.A: A globe valve gives good throttling and flow control, which is why it is used in control service.
x.B: Butterfly valves are compact but less precise for throttling steam.
x.C: Ball valves are meant for quick on/off and throttle poorly.
x.D: Gate valves are for on/off isolation, and throttling with them damages the gate.

questions.q: What happens to generator excitation when load increases?
questions.e: More load drops the terminal voltage, so excitation must increase to hold voltage.

x.A: Decreasing excitation under more load would let the voltage fall further.
x.B: Constant excitation would let the terminal voltage sag as load rises.
x.C: More load drops the terminal voltage, so excitation must be raised to hold it.
x.D: Zero excitation means no field, so the generator would produce no voltage.

questions.q: What is the term for rapid decrease in load due to sudden disconnection of a major consumer?
questions.e: Load rejection is the sudden loss of load on a generator.

x.A: Peak shaving is deliberately reducing peak demand, not a sudden loss of load.
x.B: Load rejection is the sudden loss of load on a generator.
x.C: Load shedding is deliberate disconnection of loads to protect the grid.
x.D: Load factor is a ratio over time, not an event.

questions.q: Which law of thermodynamics defines the concept of temperature?
questions.e: The zeroth law (thermal equilibrium) is the basis for temperature.

x.A: The zeroth law of thermodynamics (thermal equilibrium) is the basis for temperature.
x.B: The first law is conservation of energy.
x.C: The second law gives the direction of processes and defines entropy.
x.D: The third law deals with entropy at absolute zero.

questions.q: Which property is an intensive property of a system?
questions.e: Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of matter. Temperature is intensive; the others are extensive.

x.A: Volume depends on the amount of matter, so it is extensive.
x.B: Temperature does not depend on the amount of matter, so it is intensive.
x.C: Mass depends on the amount of matter, so it is extensive.
x.D: Total energy depends on the size of the system, so it is extensive.

questions.q: What is an example of an extensive property?
questions.e: Extensive properties depend on system size, as volume does.

x.A: Volume depends on system size, so it is extensive.
x.B: Temperature is intensive; it does not depend on system size.
x.C: Pressure is intensive; it does not depend on system size.
x.D: Density is intensive, since it is mass per unit volume.

questions.q: What is the term for a system that can exchange energy but not mass with its surroundings?
questions.e: A closed system exchanges energy (heat or work) but no mass.

x.A: A closed system exchanges energy (heat or work) but no mass.
x.B: An open system exchanges both mass and energy.
x.C: An isolated system exchanges neither mass nor energy.
x.D: An adiabatic system exchanges no heat but can still exchange mass or work.

questions.q: Which thermodynamic property is a measure of disorder?
questions.e: Entropy measures molecular disorder (randomness).

x.A: Enthalpy is the total heat content, not a measure of disorder.
x.B: Entropy measures molecular disorder or randomness.
x.C: Internal energy is the energy stored in molecules, not disorder.
x.D: Exergy is the useful work potential, not disorder.

questions.q: Which type of system does not exchange either mass or energy with its surroundings?
questions.e: An isolated system exchanges neither mass nor energy.

x.A: A closed system still exchanges energy.
x.B: An isolated system exchanges neither mass nor energy.
x.C: An open system exchanges both mass and energy.
x.D: A control volume is a region in space that can have mass crossing its boundary.

questions.q: What does the second law of thermodynamics establish?
questions.e: The second law gives the direction of natural processes. Heat flows from hot to cold without outside work.

x.A: Conservation of energy is the first law, not the second.
x.B: The second law gives the direction of natural processes: heat flows from hot to cold without outside work.
x.C: The Cp and Cv relation comes from the ideal gas relation, not the second law.
x.D: Enthalpy is a defined property (h = u + pv), not set by the second law.

questions.q: What is the term for the energy that can be converted into work?
questions.e: Exergy (available energy) is the maximum useful work obtainable.

x.A: Entropy measures disorder; it is not the energy available for work.
x.B: Enthalpy is the total heat content, and not all of it can become work.
x.C: Exergy is the maximum useful work obtainable from the energy.
x.D: Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released during a phase change.

questions.q: What is the relation between internal energy and enthalpy change for constant pressure processes?
questions.e: From h = u + pv at constant p: Δh = Δu + pΔv.

x.A: The sign is wrong: from h = u + pv at constant pressure, Δh = Δu + pΔv, so Δu would be Δh minus pΔv.
x.B: The sign is wrong: Δh is Δu plus pΔv, not minus.
x.C: From h = u + pv at constant pressure, Δh = Δu + pΔv.
x.D: This is the same relation rearranged, so it is also true; the marked answer simply writes it as Δh in terms of Δu.

questions.q: What parameters are inversely related when enthalpy is constant?
questions.e: Marked answer on the paper: pressure and volume. In a constant-enthalpy (throttling) process, an increase in one goes with a decrease in the other.

x.A: For an ideal gas at constant enthalpy the temperature stays constant, so pv is constant and pressure and volume are inversely related.
x.B: Density and pressure move together for a gas, not inversely.
x.C: Temperature and pressure at constant enthalpy depend on the Joule-Thomson effect and are not a simple inverse pair.
x.D: Volume and temperature are not simply inverse at constant enthalpy.

questions.q: What parameter primarily affects Diesel cycle efficiency?
questions.e: Marked answer on the paper. Diesel cycle efficiency depends on compression ratio and cut-off ratio, and of the choices given only cut-off ratio is a cycle parameter.

x.A: Cut-off ratio is a cycle parameter that, with compression ratio, sets Diesel cycle efficiency.
x.B: Pressure alone is not a parameter that sets Diesel cycle efficiency.
x.C: Volume alone is not a parameter that sets Diesel cycle efficiency.
x.D: Temperature alone is not a parameter that sets Diesel cycle efficiency.

questions.q: What determines the mean effective pressure in an engine cycle?
questions.e: mep = net work per cycle / displacement volume, so work per cycle is the determining factor.

x.A: Mean effective pressure is net work per cycle divided by displacement volume, so work per cycle determines it.
x.B: Fuel type affects heat release, but mep is defined by work and displacement.
x.C: Cylinder volume is only the denominator of mep.
x.D: Compression ratio affects efficiency but does not set mep by itself.

questions.q: Which device regulates the air-fuel mixture in a carbureted SI engine?
questions.e: The carburetor meters fuel into the air stream in a carbureted engine.

x.A: An injector sprays fuel in fuel-injected engines, not in a carbureted one.
x.B: A governor controls engine speed, not the mixture.
x.C: The carburetor meters fuel into the airstream in a carbureted engine.
x.D: A supercharger raises intake pressure and does not meter the mixture.

questions.q: Which cycle efficiency depends only on compression ratio?
questions.e: Otto efficiency = 1 − 1/r^(k−1), which depends only on compression ratio (and k).

x.A: Otto efficiency is 1 − 1/r^(k−1), which depends only on compression ratio (and k).
x.B: Diesel efficiency also depends on cut-off ratio.
x.C: The dual cycle depends on cut-off ratio and pressure ratio too.
x.D: The Rankine cycle depends on pressures and temperatures, not a compression ratio.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of a two-stroke engine over a four-stroke engine?
c: More power output per unit weight
questions.e: A two-stroke fires every revolution, giving a higher power-to-weight ratio.

x.A: Two-strokes are usually less efficient because some fresh charge is lost during scavenging.
x.B: A two-stroke fires every revolution, giving more power for its weight.
x.C: Two-strokes usually burn more fuel because fresh charge can escape with the exhaust.
x.D: Two-strokes tend to have dirtier exhaust, with unburned fuel and burned lubricating oil.

questions.q: Which engine efficiency is always lower than the air-standard efficiency?
questions.e: Brake efficiency includes all losses (combustion, heat, friction), so it is the lowest. Marked answer on the paper.

x.A: Thermal efficiency is a general term and can refer to indicated or brake values.
x.B: Mechanical efficiency is the ratio of brake to indicated power, not an overall efficiency.
x.C: Indicated efficiency is also below air-standard, but brake efficiency is lower still because friction losses are subtracted.
x.D: Brake efficiency includes all losses (combustion, heat and friction), so it is the lowest.

questions.q: What does the term “stoichiometric air-fuel ratio” mean?
c: Maximum air supply to minimize power
Minimum air required for complete combustion
Exact air required for complete combustion
Excess air supplied to reduce emissions
questions.e: Stoichiometric means the exact (theoretical) amount of air needed to burn the fuel completely, with no excess.

x.A: Maximum air supply is not the meaning of stoichiometric.
x.B: Minimum air is close, but the textbook meaning is the exact amount needed.
x.C: Stoichiometric means exactly the air needed for complete combustion, with no excess.
x.D: Excess air is supplied beyond stoichiometric, so it is not the definition.

questions.q: What is the effect of increasing compression ratio in SI engines?
questions.e: Otto efficiency rises with compression ratio (until knock limits it).

x.A: Efficiency does not fall as compression ratio rises.
x.B: Efficiency is not constant; it changes with compression ratio.
x.C: Otto efficiency rises with compression ratio, until knock limits it.
x.D: Efficiency depends strongly on compression ratio.

questions.q: Which type of scavenging is used in most two-stroke engines?
questions.e: Loop scavenging is the most common design in two-stroke engines. (The handwriting on your paper for this one was hard to read, so please check it.)

x.A: Cross scavenging was used in older designs with a deflector piston.
x.B: Loop scavenging is the most common design in two-stroke engines.
x.C: Uniflow scavenging is used in large engines with exhaust valves.
x.D: Radial scavenging is not a standard scavenging type.

questions.q: What is the effect of increasing cut-off ratio in a Diesel cycle?
questions.e: A larger cut-off ratio means heat is added over more of the stroke, which lowers Diesel cycle efficiency.

x.A: Efficiency does not rise with a larger cut-off ratio.
x.B: Efficiency is not constant; it changes with cut-off ratio.
x.C: A larger cut-off ratio means heat is added over more of the stroke, which lowers Diesel cycle efficiency.
x.D: Efficiency cannot double from a larger cut-off ratio.

questions.q: What is the basic mode of heat transfer in solids?
questions.e: Heat moves through solids mainly by conduction.

x.A: Conduction is the basic mode of heat transfer in solids.
x.B: Convection needs a moving fluid, so it is not the basic mode in solids.
x.C: Radiation needs no medium, but it is not the main mode inside a solid.
x.D: Advection is transport by bulk fluid flow, not heat transfer in solids.

questions.q: What law states that heat flux is proportional to the negative temperature gradient?
questions.e: Fourier's law: q = −k·dT/dx.

x.A: The Stefan-Boltzmann law is about radiation and temperature to the fourth power.
x.B: Newton's law of cooling relates convective heat transfer to temperature difference.
x.C: Fourier's law says heat flux is proportional to the negative temperature gradient.
x.D: Planck's law gives the spectrum of radiation.

questions.q: What heat transfer law states that heat transfer is proportional to temperature difference?
questions.e: Newton's law of cooling: q = hA(Ts − T∞).

x.A: The Stefan-Boltzmann law is about radiation and temperature to the fourth power.
x.B: Fourier's law is conduction, with heat flux proportional to the temperature gradient.
x.C: Newton's law of cooling: q = hA(Ts − T∞), proportional to the temperature difference.
x.D: Kirchhoff's law relates emissivity and absorptivity.

questions.q: What factor directly affects convective heat transfer?
questions.e: Higher fluid velocity thins the boundary layer and changes the convection coefficient.

x.A: Fluid velocity directly changes the boundary layer and the convection coefficient.
x.B: Density alone does not set convective heat transfer.
x.C: Pressure alone does not set convective heat transfer.
x.D: Temperature alone does not set convective heat transfer.

questions.q: What happens to the convection heat transfer coefficient when air velocity increases?
questions.e: Faster flow thins the boundary layer, so h goes up.

x.A: Faster flow thins the boundary layer, so the coefficient goes up.
x.B: The coefficient does not decrease when velocity rises.
x.C: The coefficient does not stay constant when velocity rises.
x.D: The coefficient does not become zero when velocity rises.

questions.q: Which non-dimensional number compares conduction resistance to convection resistance?
questions.e: Bi = hL/k is the ratio of internal conduction resistance to surface convection resistance.

x.A: The Reynolds number compares inertial and viscous forces.
x.B: The Nusselt number compares convection to conduction in the fluid.
x.C: Bi = hL/k compares internal conduction resistance with surface convection resistance.
x.D: The Prandtl number compares momentum and thermal diffusivity.

questions.q: Which boundary condition represents constant surface temperature?
questions.e: The Dirichlet (first-kind) condition specifies the surface temperature.

x.A: A Dirichlet condition specifies the surface temperature.
x.B: A Robin condition is a mixed condition involving convection at the surface.
x.C: A Neumann condition specifies the heat flux at the surface.
x.D: Fourier condition is not a standard name for a boundary condition.

questions.q: What is the mechanism of heat transfer in fluids due to bulk motion?
questions.e: Convection is heat transfer carried by the bulk motion of a fluid.

x.A: Conduction is molecular energy transfer without bulk motion.
x.B: Radiation is energy transfer by electromagnetic waves.
x.C: Convection is heat carried by the bulk motion of a fluid.
x.D: Evaporation is a phase change, not a heat transfer mechanism.

questions.q: Which type of convection occurs when a fan is used to cool a heated surface?
questions.e: A fan moves the fluid externally, which is forced convection.

x.A: Natural convection is driven by buoyancy, not by a fan.
x.B: A fan moves the fluid externally, which is forced convection.
x.C: Boiling convection involves a phase change, not just a fan.
x.D: Radiation is a separate mechanism, not a type of convection.

questions.q: Which dimensionless number is used to calculate radiative heat transfer between surfaces?
questions.e: Marked answer on the paper. The view factor and radiation shape factor are the same geometric quantity (F12), so check which one your reviewer prefers.

x.A: The Biot number compares conduction and convection resistance, not radiation between surfaces.
x.B: The view factor is the geometric fraction of radiation that leaves one surface and reaches another, the same quantity as the shape factor, so this is also arguably correct.
x.C: The Nusselt number is for convection.
x.D: The radiation shape factor is the geometric quantity used for radiation between surfaces (the marked answer).
